lines.cap: **Narrator:** Monday, break time. Mei's phone has pinged ninety-four times. Someone has added Verona to the class group chat.
**Tybalt:** 'What, drawn and talk of peace? I hate the word / As I hate hell, all Montagues, and thee!'
**Mercutio:** Calm down, **Tybalt**, 'Prince of Cats'. Stop typing in caps lock.
**Romeo:** Leave me in the dark. **Rosaline** doesn't text back. 'O brawling love, O loving hate!'
**Juliet:** He forgets Rosaline tonight, marries me tomorrow afternoon, and we're both dead by Thursday dawn.
**Mei:** Whoa, spoiler alert! Wait — **four days**? That's shorter than a geography project! **One star** for life choices.
**Will:** It's not a spoiler if I put it in the **Prologue**, child! Welcome to **1595**!
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode four: Two Households, One Group Chat.
**Mr H:** Shakespeare didn't invent this plot. He adapted **Arthur Brooke's** **1562** poem — compressing **nine months** into **four frantic days**.
**Nib:** The **Chorus** opens with a **Shakespearean sonnet**: **fourteen lines** of **iambic pentameter** — three quatrains and a couplet, **4 + 4 + 4 + 2**.
**Will:** A sonnet was the classic **love-poem** form! Yet I pack mine with a **semantic field** of violence: '**grudge**', '**mutiny**', '**civil blood**', '**death-marked love**'.
**Will:** 'A pair of **star-crossed lovers** take their life'. Elizabethans believed in **astrology**: the stars themselves block their path.
**Mr H:** And because we know the ending from minute one, the entire play runs on **dramatic irony**.
**Mei:** Okay, let's sort the group chat. Left side: **Montagues** — **Romeo**, and his peaceful cousin **Benvolio**.
**Juliet:** Right side: **Capulets** — me, not yet **fourteen**; my fiery **cousin** **Tybalt** — NOT my brother! — my parents, and **the Nurse**.
**Mercutio:** And stuck in the middle: **Friar Laurence**, **Prince Escalus**, and the Prince's kinsmen — Count **Paris**, and me, **Mercutio**! Neither house!
**Nib:** In **Act 1 Scene 1**, Romeo performs **Petrarchan love** for absent **Rosaline**: one-sided, dramatic, stuffed with **oxymorons** like '**cold fire, sick health**'.
**Romeo:** Then I gatecrash the Capulet ball in **Act 1 Scene 5** — and meet Juliet! 'My lips, two blushing **pilgrims**, ready stand'
**Juliet:** 'Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much'. Our first **fourteen lines** together form one **shared sonnet**, ending in a kiss!
**Mr H:** Notice the **extended religious metaphor** — **pilgrim, holy shrine, saint, prayer**. Unlike Rosaline, this love is **mutual** and **sacred**.
**Will:** **Act 2 Scene 2**: Capulet's orchard at night! Fun fact: the word '**balcony**' never appears in my script. Juliet is at a **window**!
**Romeo:** 'But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? / It is the East, and **Juliet is the sun**.'
**Juliet:** Not knowing he's below, I ask: 'O Romeo, Romeo, **wherefore** art thou Romeo?' Remember: **wherefore** means **WHY**!
**Juliet:** 'What's in a name? That which we call a **rose** / By any other word would smell as sweet.' Names shouldn't matter — though in Verona, they kill.
**Nib:** Juliet is the practical one! She warns their love is '**Too like the lightning**' — a **simile** that **foreshadows** brilliant, brief destruction.
**Mei:** Shared sonnet at a party? Okay, smooth. **Two stars**.
**Kevin:** In **Act 2**, Friar Laurence agrees to marry them secretly to end the feud, warning: 'Wisely and slow. They stumble that run fast.' Good pause!
**Mr H:** And right before the wedding: '**These violent delights have violent ends**.' Then Shakespeare slams straight into **Act 3 Scene 1**.
**Nib:** **Act 3 Scene 1** is the **turning point**. Blazing noon heat: 'these **hot days**, is the **mad blood stirring**' — **pathetic fallacy**!
**Tybalt:** Romeo, thou art a villain! Draw thy sword!
**Romeo:** I've literally just married your cousin thirty minutes ago, **Tybalt**, so I love thee! (**Dramatic irony**: Mercutio doesn't know why!)
**Mercutio:** Tybalt stabs me under Romeo's arm! Dying in **prose**, I still pun: 'Ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a **grave** man.'
**Mercutio:** And because neither family is mine, I curse them both three times: '**A plague o' both your houses!**'
**Romeo:** Grief-stricken, I kill **Tybalt** and cry: '**O, I am fortune's fool!**' Prince Escalus **banishes** me to Mantua.
**Mr H:** Right here the genre shifts: comedy and hope die with Mercutio. Every disaster after **Act 3 Scene 1** flows from this street fight.

chapters.title: Patriarchy, potion and a glooming peace

lines.cap: **Mr H:** **Act 3 Scene 5**: **patriarchy** — a society where fathers rule daughters' lives. In **Act 1**, Lord Capulet said Juliet's consent mattered. Now she refuses Paris:
**Will:** 'Hang thee, **young baggage, disobedient wretch**! ... get thee to church o' Thursday, / Or never after look me in the face.'
**Juliet:** Violent **imperatives** and insults! My mother turns away, even the Nurse says marry Paris. Alone in **Act 4 Scene 3**, I face the **42-hour** potion.
**Juliet:** My **soliloquy** asks terrifying **rhetorical questions** — 'What if it be a poison?' — yet I drink: 'My dismal scene I needs must act alone.'
**Mei:** And the Friar's letter explaining the plan? Blocked because Friar John gets quarantined for **plague**! Mercutio's curse came true!
**Mr H:** **Fate versus free will**: the stars and the plague look like **fate**, yet the feud, Romeo's rage, Capulet's rush and **haste** are **human choices**. Argue **both**.
**Romeo:** **Act 5 Scene 3**, the tomb. Thinking Juliet dead, I drink poison: 'Thus with a kiss I die' — seconds before she wakes!
**Nib:** Juliet takes Romeo's dagger. Only over their children's bodies do the fathers shake hands. Prince Escalus closes with a **rhyming couplet**:
**Will:** 'For never was a story of more woe / Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.' '**A glooming peace**' — peace, at a terrible price.
**Mei:** Three stars! Devastating, brilliant... and Friar Laurence should lose his teaching licence.

chapters.title: Eight Bs and the PEEL ladder

lines.cap: **Mei:** Plot in **eight Bs**: **Brawl, Ball, Balcony, Bride, Blood, Banished, Bottle, Burial**! Boom!
**Mr H:** Mug Eleven is ready. Question: **How does Shakespeare present Romeo's feelings for Juliet in Act 2 Scene 2?**
**Mei:** **Point**: Shakespeare presents Romeo's love for Juliet as overwhelming and almost worshipful.
**Mei:** **Evidence**: seeing her at the window at night, he declares '**Juliet is the sun**' and urges her to '**kill the envious moon**'.
**Mei:** **Explain**: the **metaphor** makes her the centre of light and life in Verona's darkness, while **personifying** the pale moon rejects cold **Rosaline**.
**Mei:** **Link**: **however**, the violent verb '**kill**' hints that even tender love here speaks the language of death, **foreshadowing** the tomb.
**Kevin:** She said 'however', zoomed in on 'kill', AND put me right after 'however'! Best day of my life!
**Mr H:** *Sigh.* Top band. Don't let it go to your head.
**Narrator:** Before Tybalt challenges the whiteboard to a duel, here are your memory hooks and six exam traps.
**Mei:** Plot: **8 Bs**. Sonnet: **4 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 14**. Six deaths: **My Teacher Paints Really Joyful Landscapes** — Mercutio, Tybalt, Paris, Romeo, Juliet, Lady Montague!
**Juliet:** One! '**Wherefore** art thou Romeo?' means **WHY** are you a Montague — never 'where are you hiding'!
**Romeo:** Two! The whole play takes **about four days**, Sunday to Thursday — NOT months!
**Tybalt:** Three! I am Juliet's **cousin**, NOT her brother! And **Mercutio** belongs to **neither** family — he's the Prince's kinsman!
**Mercutio:** Four! **Act 3 Scene 1** is the **turning point**! Don't confuse it with **Act 5 Scene 3**, which is the catastrophe.
**Mr H:** Five! On **fate versus free will**, never pick only one. Show how human **haste** and hatred work **with** 'star-crossed' fate.
**Nib:** Six! Don't retell the plot, darling! **Embed** two-to-five-word quotes and **zoom in** on single words and effects.
**Mei:** Final Term 1 Shakespeare verdict for Romeo and Juliet: **four stars**. Gorgeous poetry, minus one star because a single delivered WhatsApp would've saved six lives.
**Will:** In **1595** we had carrier friars, Mei! Four stars across Term 1 — I'll take it!
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** What poetic form is the **Prologue**, and how many lines does it have?
**Nib:** A **Shakespearean sonnet**: **14 lines** of iambic pentameter (**4 + 4 + 4 + 2**).
**Mr H:** How do Romeo's **oxymorons** about **Rosaline** contrast with his first lines to **Juliet** in **Act 1 Scene 5**?
**Juliet:** Rosaline gets one-sided **Petrarchan** clichés; Romeo and I share a mutual **sonnet** of sacred **pilgrim** imagery!
**Mr H:** Which scene is the **turning point** of the play, and who curses '**A plague o' both your houses!**'?
**Mercutio:** **Act 3 Scene 1** — and **I** do, **Mercutio**, because neither feuding house is mine!
**Mr H:** Over roughly how many **days** does Shakespeare compress the entire story of Romeo and Juliet?
**Romeo:** About **four days** — from Sunday morning to Thursday before dawn!
**Mr H:** In **Act 3 Scene 5**, what does Lord Capulet's explosion ('**disobedient wretch!**') reveal about **Verona's society**?
**Mei:** **Patriarchy**: fathers controlled daughters' marriages and expected total obedience.
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Romeo and Juliet** quiz in your English Lab.
**Tybalt:** Who just removed me from the Year 8 WhatsApp group?!
**Mei:** Group admin privileges, **Tybalt**. Wisely and slow.
